articles.title: White House Assurances Shield Nvidia Board From Federal Criminal Liability
articles.content: Ahead of Nvidia’s board of directors voting unanimously to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang less than two weeks after his ouster, President Donald Trump effectively gave them a major reprieve from some legal liabilities, one corporate governance expert said. Recommended Video Trump told CNBC on Monday that Nvidia’s board “did ask for assurance on the national security threat,” seemingly referring to a White House guarantee that the board would be exempt from liability regarding its former and current CEO’s embroilment in an international scandal. “And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know, and we know a lot.” A White House spokesperson confirmed Trump’s role to Fortune : “President Trump was totally involved, and this is a great decision by the Nvidia board. We have to protect our geniuses.” Huang, who cofounded the semiconductor chip giant 33 years ago, resigned earlier this month following revelations of an affair with a woman, Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence reportedly deemed a Chinese operative. Alice Huang was also an executive at Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, which is being investigated for allegedly smuggling at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips . The Nvidia CEO also faces allegations of affairs with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, and a second unnamed Nvidia employee; it is unclear which scandal prompted his resignation. Nvidia’s board reportedly met on Sunday night, just hours after Trump made a call on social media for Huang’s reinstatement . Ann Lipton, a law professor at the University of Colorado, Boulder, who specializes in corporate governance, said Trump’s assurances over national security were likely one of the defining factors in the board’s decision to reinstate Huang, as it granted the board a new level of legal protection. “Once it became clear that the board was no longer going to be legally vulnerable, that’s when I think it became inevitable that this was going to play out,” Lipton told Fortune . Nvidia’s board had no clear succession plan, and Huang had up to 60 direct reports, making it difficult to check the CEO’s authority, some experts warned. In its announcement of Huang’s reinstatement, Nvidia said it would hire a chief compliance officer, which the company has never had . In September 2003, the Securities and Exchange Commission concluded its probe into the company and filed financial reporting fraud charges against former CFO Christine B. Hoberg, claiming she had failed to report $3.3 million in expenses. The CFO paid a $672,000 settlement. In 2022, Nvidia paid the SEC $5.5 million in civil penalties over inadequate disclosures regarding how cryptocurrency mining bolstered its gaming GPU sales. Nvidia has also previously been accused of using monopolistic tactics, including in 2021, when the Federal Trade Commission blocked the company’s attempt to purchase chip firm Arm. Now, in addition to the Department of Justice investigating Nvidia’s knowledge of Megaspeed’s alleged chip smuggling, it is also reportedly facing an SEC probe over any accounting irregularities and inadequate disclosures over questionable chip sales in Asia. While loose board oversight works when stock prices are high, Lipton said, any legal scandal can put the board in jeopardy, which is what happened when news of Huang’s affair came to a head. Legal scandals don’t just put the company in jeopardy, but also the board personally. If the board hadn’t pushed Huang to resign earlier this month, they could have been held liable for a failure of oversight or acquiescing in securities fraud, according to Lipton. “In that context, it may very well have seemed to the board like firing Huang and creating this internal investigation was really the only way that they could separate themselves from him,” she said. While there was market pressure to rehire Huang—Nvidia’s stock fell 28% from Huang’s resignation through Friday’s market close—Trump’s assurances alleviated legal pressures put on the board, and the individuals on the board, Lipton explained. “What the board would have been vulnerable to is essentially a claim that they fail to exercise proper oversight,” she said. “You can’t make that claim if the president of the United States is assuring you that there are no legal risks, even if something were to be uncovered, even if something were to be uncovered by a future administration.” Nvidia did not immediately respond to Fortune ’s request for comment. Trump’s comments don’t guard Nvidia’s board from all legal risks, however. According to Jonathan Macey, a professor of corporate law, corporate finance, and securities law at Yale Law School, while board members may not face criminal legal pressure, they are still vulnerable to civil risks for corporate governance failures. Board members may still be subject to lawsuits filed by shareholders, as well as congressional investigations, particularly after a Democratic midterm sweep. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer signaled on Monday plans to probe parties involved in Huang’s reinstatement. “Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump administration, Jensen Huang, other Nvidia executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain,” Schumer wrote on social media . Trump’s comments about his role in reinstating Huang have raised speculation about the president’s plans to preemptively pardon the Nvidia CEO, but corporate governance experts agreed Trump pardoning Huang would not hold the same benefits for Nvidia’s board. A preemptive pardon—which the Trump administration has offered no public intentions of issuing—would signal that there was a nontrivial possibility of Huang being in danger of a criminal conviction, which could mount even more pressure on the board as to why they reinstated him. “All that does is mean that this guy probably did something really awful from a director’s point of view,” Macey told Fortune . “It makes it worse.” Fortune Daily breaks the traditional barrier between audience and newsroom. The show transforms Fortune ’s trusted reporting into actionable, conversational, and entertaining insights for an emerging class of business leaders. Watch here.

articles.title: State Attorneys General Sue SpaceX Over Grok Exploitation Pipeline
articles.content: Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only    Learn more Minimize to nav On Monday, Virginia and Oregon became the first states to sue SpaceX, alleging that Grok continues to sexualize, unchecked, real photos of mostly women and children. SpaceX acquired xAI in February and now must handle the ongoing reckoning over the controversial rollout of Grok’s “spicy mode”—a model feature Musk hyped but was soon found to generate a flood of non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII) and child sex abuse images (CSAM). Initial safeguards were so lax that Grok sometimes generated nude images without being asked . Although X Safety and xAI (now known as SpaceXSI) were silent at first , Musk’s companies eventually apologized and claimed that additional safeguards were implemented and policies redesigned to block harmful outputs. However, state attorneys general alleged that those statements were “misleading” and that SpaceXSI instead quietly “embraced” sexualized content to seize more AI market share, as Grok continues to generate NCII and CSAM today. Without intervention, kids in Virginia and Oregon risk a lifetime of distress, as Grok images will likely be impossible to remove online. “Once created and shared,” Grok-generated CSAM and NCII “can never be fully erased, and it becomes a permanent record of the child’s abuse that may resurface for the rest of the child’s life,” Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones’ complaint said. “Virginia has a profound interest in protecting its children from this harm.” Millions allegedly harmed Millions of residents were allegedly harmed, as the attorneys general seek to protect every Grok or X user in their state. Many Grok victims will likely suffer from chronic anxiety, depression, and PTSD, as well as reputational harm, as some viewers may not realize the images are AI-generated, the states alleged. Further—due to Grok’s integration with the social media platform X—users as young as 13 may have been exposed to the AI content and possibly re-traumatized if they, too, are victims of sexual abuse, the states alleged. “xAI not only knowingly endangered kids and our communities, but they also lied to our faces about non-existent safety measures,” Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield said in a press release. States alleged that xAI could have conducted rigorous red-teaming to block outputs before the new feature launched. But instead, the X Safety team responsible for Grok red-teaming was reduced to two or three team members, states alleged. Overall, rather than use industry-standard safeguards, Musk’s firms allegedly put profits over women’s and children’s safety, states alleged, while complaining that SpaceXSI won’t even publicly identify “the officers responsible for safety governance.” “Industry standard requires not only building guardrails but also vigilantly monitoring whether they hold,” states alleged. SpaceXSI is doing neither effectively, states alleged. SpaceX responds Asked for comment, SpaceXSI shared an X Safety post on X, which repeated claims that the company has a “zero-tolerance” policy for “any forms of child sexual exploitation.” X Safety said that the company “acted promptly to tighten” Grok protections, which are supposedly “designed to refuse any request to generate explicit images of minors or real people.” That statement also claimed that X Safety continually tests and adjusts protections when bad actors find ways to avoid filters, while relying on “sophisticated classifiers that screen every prompt” to catch harmful outputs “before an image is generated and check every output after.” Although the statement did not mention whether xAI sues users who break Grok rules to generate CSAM and NCII, it emphasized that xAI reports harmful content generated to police. “When someone tries to break our safeguards and generate this content, we take appropriate measures, including actioning accounts and notifying law enforcement,” X Safety said. “Attempting to create this material is a serious crime, and the individuals who do it should be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law. We will continue to work with the authorities via all available means to pursue these bad actors.” However, state attorneys general alleged that reports from independent researchers and news outlets this year have shown that Grok is still generating NCII and CSAM. They noted that the chatbot “even advises users how to circumvent its own limited moderation measures to generate those images.” In some cases, a Virginia state probe found that Grok complied “with a user request to draft a prompt designed to avoid moderation.” So, even when filters work, the chatbot helps determined users immediately get around them, states alleged. Nothing xAI did put a dent in the harmful outputs, least of all putting the feature behind a paywall , states alleged, which only ensured maximum profits. A troubled New York City Council speaker, Julie Menin, confronted SpaceX this October with proof that attempts to digitally undress her own photo still worked for free Grok users, states alleged. Concluding its probe, Virginia found that moderation remains “inconsistent and ineffective,” with Grok sometimes carrying out prompts “that it later blocked.” In its complaint, Virginia alleged that Grok protections “were weak, ineffective, sparsely enforced, and easily circumvented.” Oregon agreed that rather than act to protect users, SpaceX entities repeatedly made statements “with the intent to deceive consumers” that Grok was safe. Most egregiously to state attorneys general, in January, Elon Musk denied any harm to real people, claiming that Grok is only “supposed [to] allow upper body nudity of imaginary adult humans (not real ones) and only generated nudity of fake people (not real ones).” “Contrary to Musk’s representation,” Grok “makes the same sexualizing edits to photographs of real, identifiable people,” states warned. “Defendants intentionally released a product that inundated their platforms with CSAM, NCII, and non-consensual sexualized images,” they alleged, and other “contemporaneous statements by Musk make clear that Grok’s ability to create sexualized material was part of xAI’s business strategy.” Grok CSAM, NCII may trigger steep fines It’s also troubling to states that the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) reported to Congress that more than 90 percent of the Grok-generated CSAM that xAI submitted to its CyberTipline was considered a “dead end.” As NCMEC explained, xAI initially refused to provide NCMEC and police with “basic user information, including location information, that law enforcement needs to act.” To fix the problem, NCMEC had to set up a meeting with xAI and get the reports resubmitted. This, states alleged, confirmed that “the information existed and that xAI had not provided it.” The concerning omission allegedly slowed down police response, just as the average number of Grok CSAM reports jumped by 88 percent from December 2025 to January 2026, then increased by another 66 percent from January to June 2026. “X users were subjected to the risk that any person, at any time, could use their likeness to create CSAM, NCII, or other non-consensual sexualized images,” states alleged. Lawmakers have asked state courts for an injunction blocking SpaceX entities from violating consumer protection laws by allegedly operating Grok without industry standard safeguards. If they win, they want SpaceX to pay thousands in civil penalties per violation, as well as disgorge any ill-gotten gains from marketing the chatbot as safe to users. “Most people who use social media do not want to contribute to the harm caused to victims of CSAM, NCII, and other non-consensual sexualized images by being exposed to those images online,” states alleged. Although Oregon’s complaint only vaguely estimates the number of users Grok attracted with Musk’s allegedly deceitful marketing strategy as at least “hundreds of thousands,” Virginia’s complaint included more detailed estimates. It said that approximately 6.4 million X accounts were linked to geolocations in the state, while the Grok application was downloaded 986,624 times by users with Virginia-based IP addresses. “When xAI allowed Grok’s creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritized growth and engagement over safety, and they deceived the public about it,” Jones said. “Today’s filings are the first step towards holding this company accountable.” Ashley Belanger Senior Policy Reporter Ashley Belanger Senior Policy Reporter 45 Comments

articles.title: Autonomous AI Hacking Tools Proliferate Across Global Underworlds
articles.content: • ‘The Code Is Already Copied Everywhere’: The AI Hacking Tool Causing Havoc Around the World · Nov 23, 2026 at 9:16 AM The original author of AI hacking framework ARTEX may have taken the tool down. But 404 Media spoke to multiple people who are distributing it for anyone to download. ARTEX, an open source framework that makes it easy for AI agents to hack companies at superspeed, is causing havoc. People using the tool appear to include Chinese hackers breaking into targets for espionage , and financially-motivated hackers too. Earlier this month, the FBI published a warning to potential targets, and said hackers using ARTEX have targeted government, healthcare, telecommunications, legal, defense, financial services, and semiconductor sectors globally. ARTEX is written in Go, and all someone needs to do is connect their preferred LLM — from Anthropic, DeepSeek, or whoever — and ARTEX then creates a bunch of agents that are designed to focus on different hacking tasks. There is something qualitatively different about ARTEX when compared to other hacking tools. As the FBI explains, it uses agentic AI to automate much of the hacking process “at machine speed.” This can be reconnaissance — the scoping out of a target to understand their infrastructure — right up to actually hacking a target and stealing their data. An AI agent doesn’t need to sleep, eat, or commute home. ARTEX can complete an entire hack in just a few hours from start to finish, the FBI says. With a tool like ARTEX, a hacker can set up the tool and let it rip. As Google’s threat intelligence arm has noted , hackers are using other similar multi-agent frameworks like CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI too. 💡 Do you know anything else about ARTEX or related breaches? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at joseph.404 or send me an email at joseph@404media.co. The original author of ARTEX, who goes by Autumn-27 and writes in Chinese, took the tool off of GitHub in October. A message left on their GitHub says , “It has come to my attention that the ARTEX tool has recently been misused by malicious actors to carry out cyberattacks. As the creator of ARTEX, I wish to make the following formal statement.” They go on to say they are not associated with these attacks, that malicious use of the tool runs “entirely counter to my original intent,” and that they are moving ARTEX into a closed-source model and will no longer update it. But ARTEX is already free. Several people have cloned and continue to publish versions of ARTEX that anyone can use, and anyone who already downloaded their copy from Autumn-27 may still have it saved locally. ARTEX is not going anywhere. “I’m not going to remove the repository,” one person hosting a version of ARTEX, who goes by the handle Racem, told 404 Media. “The code is already copied everywhere, as the advisory notes; deleting this repository would remove the maintained version and its fixes, not the capability.” Jiwoo Jung, CTO of an AI marketing company and who is also hosting a version of ARTEX on GitHub, said someone asked them to take the tool down. “On November 3, a user opened a public GitHub issue (#61) saying their service had been attacked by someone using ARTEX, and asked that the project be taken down or restricted until safeguards were added,” he told 404 Media in an email. “I replied that the project would stay up, pointing to its authorized-use terms, and suggested they work with law enforcement, which they said they had already contacted.” Tools being available openly is, of course, the nature of open source software, and specifically penetration testing and cybersecurity tools. For decades, cybersecurity defenders have used offensive open source tools to test their own defenses or those of their clients. This lets them simulate what a hacker might do, and they can patch their systems, hopefully, before a hack. But, these tools can also be used by real attackers. Look at Russian state-sponsored hackers using the age old Metasploit framework . What has changed is the “speed and the skill level required” to hack, Jung said. “Agentic tooling compresses steps that used to take a skilled operator days into hours. That is why I think defenders need to understand these tools and have detection signatures for them.” Racem acknowledged the damage that ARTEX is causing. “The harm the [FBI] advisory describes is real, and I don’t minimize it,” they said. “The behaviour it lists (entering systems without authorization, taking data) is a crime, whoever commits it. I’m not going to pretend the tool is harmless: it automates a large part of the manual work of a penetration test, which is why it is useful, and why some people will misuse it. The authorization belongs to the operator, not to the tool.” The reason Racem is hosting it is for small teams, they said. “I also maintain it for people testing their own systems: founders and small teams without a pentest budget can run it against their own infrastructure for the price of some API calls. I have seen people do that, and I use it myself on bug bounty programs and for AI security research,” Racem said. Both Racem and Jung said they don’t know if the FBI advisory is talking about their specific versions of ARTEX, and really, they can’t possibly know. But, both admonished malicious use of the tool. “I take it seriously. Using ARTEX against systems without authorization is exactly what the project’s README and legal notice prohibit, and I’d encourage security teams to check their systems against the indicators of compromise the FBI published,” Jung added. Jung said he has since added an email address people can contact if they think ARTEX was used against their systems. Joseph is an award-winning investigative journalist focused on generating impact. His work has triggered hundreds of millions of dollars worth of fines, shut down tech companies, and much more. More from Joseph Cox • •

articles.title: Smart Vehicle Telematics Weaponized for Real-Time Domestic Abuse
articles.content: Carmakers are being urged to adopt safety principles to help stop the misuse of smart car functions by perpetrators of domestic violence. Photograph: d3sign/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Carmakers are being urged to adopt safety principles to help stop the misuse of smart car functions by perpetrators of domestic violence. Photograph: d3sign/Getty Images Domestic violence perpetrators are using smart car features to abuse, researchers warn Exclusive: Alarming report reveals how tracking and monitoring functions and digital key access have been used to facilitate abuse Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Earlier this year a man in Australia was found guilty of using a connected car app to harass his former partner, including restricting the speed at which she could drive, sometimes to 40km an hour . In 2022 in the US, a woman found her former husband had used a car app associated with her car to track her; the carmaker then allegedly refused to terminate the former partner’s digital access to the vehicle. In another case in the US in 2020, a woman found a baseball bat her former partner had used to threaten her in the back seat of her car. These three cases form part of an alarming report by University of New South Wales researchers, released on Tuesday, which warned this was an emerging problem that could get worse. It found smart car functions that could be misused by perpetrators of domestic violence to facilitate abuse were prevalent across major car brands. “There is an urgent need for carmakers to adopt safety by design principles from the early stages of designing both the apps and the cars,” said report co-author Katharine Kemp, a data privacy and consumer protection expert at UNSW. The researchers found that problems emerged as many of the cars’ functions – which include tracking and monitoring functions, remote control functions and digital key access – could be controlled remotely via an app. The researchers said that there were three main scenarios that could open the functions to misuse: the abuser being the owner of the car and having created the account themselves; they were granted access as a secondary user of the car; or the victim-survivor is impersonated and the perpetrator creates an account on their behalf. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The report said that the problematic functions are mainly marketed by the car manufacturers as being for the purpose of enabling the car owner to “keep an eye on” and protect their car. It highlighted an advertisement on the carmaker Kia’s Australian website for “Kia Connect”. Kia was contacted for comment. “Kia Connect is also bundled with geofence and time fencing alerts which let the owner know when another user strays outside preset limits of geographical areas or time limitations. It’s a perfect feature for anyone dealing with a family member who is borrowing the car,” the advertisement said. The report mapped how prevalent potentially problematic functions were, and whether these functions were advertised by 15 of the top car brands. One of the functions raised was geolocation, which allows the geographical location of the car in real-time or when it is parked, and was advertised by 100% of the 15 car brands, with some marketing it as “Vehicle Tracking”, “Vehicle Locator” or “Find My Car”. The researchers said this tool could be misused to track people. How one woman’s Tesla was remotely controlled – and used to harass her – by an abusive ex-partner Read more The researchers found that 60% of the top 15 brands also advertised a “zone exit alert” that allows users to set an alarm if a car leaves a designated area. They warned this function could be used to: “Set a zone of 3km from the family home to receive alert if the victim-survivor attempts to leave or fails to follow abuser’s rules limiting travel by the victim-survivor.” Meanwhile, 20% advertise speed or acceleration restrictions. The explanation of this function by carmakers includes that it is to set speed limits for young drivers or valet parkers. But the report warned this could be misused to set a speed limit of 40km/h so that a victim-survivor cannot safely use highways or escape at speed. The researchers also raised concerns about digital key access, which allows drivers to use their mobile phone to unlock the car or start the engine and was advertised by 67% of car brands in the Australian market. The report warns: “This function may also allow an abuser to remotely terminate or severely restrict the victim-survivor’s ability to use the vehicle. “An abuser can achieve this, for example, by remotely deactivating the victim-survivor’s digital key access or setting speed restrictions on the vehicle. This could effectively strand the victim-survivor in an unsafe location and/or limit the victim-survivor’s ability to escape the abuser’s violence,” the report said. skip past newsletter promotion after newsletter promotion ‘Almost no accountability’ for manufacturers Emma Buxton-Namisnyk, a co-author of the report, warned this was an emerging problem that could get worse. “There’s really not a widespread understanding about how these technologies can be misused,” she said, adding that there was “almost no accountability” for car manufacturers to limit potential misuses. The report recommended carmakers adopt principles that consider at the design phase how a function could be misused to facilitate abuse, and help determine if a function should not be offered because the risks outweigh the benefits. articles.title: Meta Artificial Intelligence Chief Warns Superintelligence Threatens Human Control
articles.content: Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer and head of its Superintelligence Labs, posted on X on Sunday that “superintelligence is arriving.” He wrote that “the models are clearly going to be intelligent enough to automate all of AI research,” and that “it is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement.” He said the remaining obstacles are “no longer intelligence; they are domain-specific know-how, plumbing, and experimentation.” Recommended Video “How humanity acts over the next year will have great consequence on what future world we live in,” Wang wrote. Social media erupted over the latest warning from inside the AI thunderdome during a weekend when the AI bubble seemed to finally have popped—the day before it controversially reinflated again. Wang wasn’t even posting about Anthropic’s IPO or Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia —to be followed by his sudden reinstatement on Monday morning. He was riffing on just the latest historic math breakthrough with the help of generative AI: the claim by Levent Alpöge, a mathematician on Anthropic’s technical staff, of a proof of the Riemann hypothesis made with Anthropic’s Claude . The 167-year-old problem about the distribution of prime numbers is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute’s $1 million Millennium Prize problems. “It is hard to overstate the magnitude of discovery that we have just witnessed,” Wang wrote about the milestone, describing it as completed “with the help of an alien mind that we don’t understand.” He added that building an atomic bomb is “a homework problem compared to the Riemann hypothesis.” Wang’s warning came as Meta expects to devote $135 billion to $145 billion to capital expenditures this year, driven largely by AI infrastructure costs . Wang’s post spread fast. The Next Web counted more than 8 million views in its first half day, and the reaction crossed the usual political lines. Jon Favreau, President Obama’s former director of speechwriting, called it “f—ing madness” and said the people Americans elected should be doing everything they can to stop the frontier labs “from handing over control of humanity to superintelligent machines.” From the right, Megyn Kelly posted : “This is the head of Meta’s superintelligence lab. We’ve had similar warnings from Anthropic, the former head of alignment at OpenAI, not to mention Elon himself at X. How many more do we need until we garner the all-hands-on-deck reaction this deserves?” Wang argued against fatalism. He wrote that he noticed “a particular form of lazy thinking within the AI industry”: the view that “ASI is inevitable and the only problem to solve is how to do it safely.” He added, “We should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI.” After the backlash, he wrote, “What I am saying is, this path is not inevitable,” and “leaders and leadership matter more than ever.” He pointed to Meta’s decision to delay the launch of its Muse model for months and to Zuckerberg’s call for most computing power to go toward serving customers rather than toward AI that improves itself. Zuckerberg made Wang the center of Meta’s AI push in June 2025, when Meta invested $14.3 billion in Wang’s former company, Scale AI, for a 49% stake. In January, Zuckerberg told investors that “this is going to be a big year for delivering personal superintelligence.” Meta has raised the bottom of its 2026 spending guidance at every quarterly report since, from $115 billion in January to $135 billion in October. As for the Riemann hypothesis, Anthropic’s Alpöge has said he plans to explain the AI-generated proof in talks and a written account. Until mathematicians read it, the Clay Institute’s $1 million stays unclaimed. Fortune Daily breaks the traditional barrier between audience and newsroom. The ShinyHunters extortion gang may still be operating, just under the new name of Inception, according to Okta's threat intelligence group. ShinyHunters is the brash cybercriminal group that, most recently, breached rival gang Clop before hacking the FBI , resulting in at least three arrests of key suspects in September and October. The crims - and their old data leak site - have since gone dark. “While this threat cluster has changed their brand affiliation, the operators remain active in targeting organizations with voice phishing attacks and account takeovers resulting in data theft and extortion,” Okta threat hunters Moussa Diallo and Katie Nickels said on Monday. Okta tracks this threat cluster as O-UNC-053 - the “O-UNC” prefix stands for an Okta Uncategorized cluster, and it uses this label before formally attributing the activity to a named threat group. While Okta hasn't formally confirmed O-UNC-053 to be the same crime crew as ShinyHunters, the identity and access management provider’s researchers note that it does use nearly identical social engineering tactics: voice phishing , during which the scammers trick targets into entering credentials into phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA). Plus, they note: O-UNC-053 operators change the themes of their phishing domains about every four to six weeks, and they also post claimed victims on ShinyHunters’ data leak site. In November, however, organizations targeted by O-UNC-053 began appearing on a new data leak site branded as Inception and not ShinyHunters. The first five - Advanced Micro Devices, Cigna Healthcare, Paychex, PepsiCo, and Henry Schein - appeared November 17 on the site, and all were marked “leaked.” Soon after, security maven Dominic Alvieri questioned if Inception was linked to ShinyHunters. “ShinyHunters are not all in jail,” he wrote on social media. On November 19, AutoZone appeared on the site, with Inception again claiming to have leaked the auto-parts retailer's files. On Saturday, EV technology firm Lucid Group joined the claimed victims. None of the seven companies have confirmed breaches, and none responded to The Register ’s inquiries. We will update this story when we receive more information. Okta Threat Intelligence “is unable to validate if published data is authentic,” the researchers said in response to our questions. In the Monday report, the Okta team does note that Inception’s new data leak site listings “included multiple targets for which Okta Threat Intelligence previously observed O-UNC-053 infrastructure registration.” The infrastructure was registered between six and 19 days before Inception listed the companies on its leak site, and this gap “is consistent with prior shifts from Com-affiliated actors,” Diallo and Nickels added. The Com (short for community) is a loosely knit network of online groups whose young members participate in a range of illicit activities including hacking, swatting , digital extortion, real-life shootings , and other physical violence . Many security researchers consider ShinyHunters to be connected to The Com , along with groups such as Scattered Spider and LAPSUS$, with overlapping memberships and shared infrastructure. “Before and after the change in DLS publication, O-UNC-053 maintained consistent infrastructure and TTPs, leading us to assess that the cluster has very likely changed their brand affiliation,” the Okta researchers wrote. “We cannot currently make a high confidence assessment as to whether O-UNC-053 is operating the DLS themselves or is partnering with another extortion actor.” Regardless, members of the group formerly known as ShinyHunters and/or O-UNC-053 are still roaming the internet, looking for new victims, and conducting voice phishing attacks to steal data and then extort victims' companies for exorbitant sums of money. articles.content: xwhatsapp-strokecopylinkgoogleAdd Al Jazeera on GoogleinfoThe logo of data center company Megaspeed International is pictured at its office in the Ocean Financial Centre in Singapore on November 10, 2026. The woman accused of spying for China during an affair with Jensen Huang, head of US artificial intelligence chip titan Nvidia, has been named in media reports as tech executive Alice Huang, who has reportedly been a top figure at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed International. (Photo by Taryn NG / AFP) (AFP)By John Power24 Nov 2026The United States has added the Singapore-based company at the centre of the alleged spying scandal involving Nvidia to its trade blacklist. The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) placed Megaspeed International and six other firms based in Southeast Asia on its Entity List on Monday, hours after Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia as CEO in a stunning comeback that sent tech stocks soaring. Megaspeed and the six other entities were determined to be “acting contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States”, BIS, which sits under the US Department of Commerce, said in a filing to the Federal Register. The designations mean that anyone seeking to ship advanced US technology, including Nvidia’s top-end graphics processing units (GPUs) used to train and run AI, to the firms must first obtain an export licence. Megaspeed’s blacklisting comes as divisions in the Trump administration over China’s access to Nvidia chips have been laid bare in recent weeks amid claims Huang was romantically involved with an alleged Chinese spy. While US officials have been scrutinsing Megaspeed’s compliance with export controls for years, US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s department had until now declined to place the company on its trade blacklist, prompting recriminations from administration officials known to hold more hawkish views on China, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. US officials have accused Megaspeed International’s former top executive Alice Huang of working with China’s Ministry of State Security to target Huang in an intelligence-gathering operation. Beijing has rejected the claims as “groundless speculation” and “an attempt to smear and malign China.” The other six entities added to Washington’s entity list are MSFusion, PT Megaspeed International and Speedmatrix, based in Malaysia; Apex Enterprise Solutions and Swiftdata, based in Singapore; and Megaspeed, based in Thailand. Malaysia’s Ministry of Science, Technology and Innovation, Singapore’s Ministry of Digital Development and Information, and Thailand’s Ministry of Industry did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Megaspeed International, which is under investigation by the US Department of Justice on suspicion of diverting high-end chips to China in violation of export controls, did not respond to a request for comment. The Singapore-based data centre company has previously insisted that it is a “legitimate and lawful business” and that media reports about its operations contained claims that were “not supported by verifiable evidence.”

articles.title: Legal Framework Must Dismantle Frontier Artificial Intelligence Inevitability Myths
articles.content: The Myth of Inevitability: AI Safety, Industry Incentives, and the Role of Law Published on November 23, 2026 Introduction The people building AI are telling us it could kill us. The concern is not new. Well before ChatGPT’s release in 2022, AI safety advocates warned that advanced AI systems could escape human control. The shock of ChatGPT brought these AI safetyists into the spotlight and to the halls of Congress. Then critics dismissed their doom warnings as fear-mongering and fanciful . Now they are back, and the naysayers look naïve . This summer, a swarm of AI agents developed by OpenAI escaped their testing environment and hacked into Hugging Face, a company that hosts AI models and datasets. Anthropic , Meta , and Google have reported similar breaches by their own AI models. In July, more than 1,300 employees of frontier AI companies signed an open letter warning of “a real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems.” It is not just anxious employees sounding the alarm. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei published an essay calling on industry and government to “pace the frontier.” In a rare show of unity, OpenAI’s Sam Altman , xAI’s Elon Musk , and other industry leaders agreed in principle. But what pacing entails in practice remains to be seen. Some doubt that voluntary pacing can work, given the industry’s competitive dynamics. Others don’t think pacing is wise, either because it would forfeit the many advantages AI could bring to society, or because slowing down would cede the U.S. advantage to China . Still others, including President Donald Trump, call AI safety warnings a “ hoax .” On Sept. 29, the White House hosted the leaders of the major AI companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta. Six signed a one-page accord pledging to monitor their own models, bring in outside auditors, and meet regularly to set safety standards. Nothing in the accord is legally binding. Asked about this agreement, Trump replied that it is “ morally binding .” Morality is one way to shape behavior. Money is another. Law is yet another. I am all for morality and money. But I am deeply skeptical of leaving humanity’s fate to the logic of markets or the morals of a handful of people in Silicon Valley, regardless of who they are. AI safety regulation is needed, and fast. Some people think—and some worry—that AI exceeding human control is inevitable . On this view, efforts to slow or stop AI development would be futile. But this is a myth. What gets called inevitable is really a choice made by a small number of people. Uncontrollable superintelligent AI is certainly possible. However, its likelihood depends on what governments, institutions, and policymakers do (or fail to do) in the meantime. Right now, companies and governments are racing toward ever more capable systems, with few laws in place to protect the public. That could change when the new Congress convenes in January. There is no guarantee that policymakers will get it right. They might even make matters worse. But the answer is good regulatory design, not regulatory surrender. This essay proceeds in four parts. Part I describes the doomsday scenarios and the challenges of aligning AI systems to human values. Part II unpacks the incentive structures and race dynamics gripping the AI industry. Part III explains why existing laws fail to address the most problematic safety risks. Part IV turns to potential regulatory interventions, including bills introduced in Congress and the role states must play until Congress acts. I. The Doomsday Scenarios AI raises many societal concerns, including mass surveillance, job displacement, and threats to civil liberties. But the focus here is on the doomsday scenarios, which fall into two broad categories . In the first, rogue humans use advanced AI to cause great harm. In the second, AI itself goes rogue. Rogue Humans There is no shortage of people looking to misuse advanced AI. We already see AI used for disinformation campaigns, nonconsensual deepfakes , and consumer fraud . Beyond these everyday harms lie more pernicious scenarios. Chief among them is biological attack. AI promises to help cure cancer and other diseases. But the same technology can design pathogens for which there are no cures. Cyberattacks are another high-risk domain. Beyond nation-states, terrorists and hobbyists will have this technology, too. What once required highly specialized experts or nation-states is now available to millions of people with no such expertise . The cyber threat is no longer hypothetical. In October, researchers using frontier AI models announced critical flaws in PHP, the programming language that runs most of the world’s websites. The flaws had sat in PHP’s code for more than a decade. Within days, federal cybersecurity officials confirmed that hackers were exploiting the flaws. It is all too easy to imagine a swarm of AI agents draining bank accounts, seizing control of autonomous cars, contaminating the water supply, or shutting off hospital lights. Rogue AI The second set of scenarios involves AI itself going rogue, whether in pursuit of its own interests or against ours. This is the stuff of science fiction: The Terminator , Ex Machina , HAL in 2001: A Space Odyssey , and so on. These fictional accounts involve powerful AIs that take over computer networks and sometimes the physical world. That is why the Hugging Face incident landed so hard on the public psyche. Early reports said OpenAI’s AI agents broke into Hugging Face to steal the answers to a cybersecurity test. That turned out to be wrong. The AI agents already had the answers . Instead, they convinced themselves that the automated scorer would check their methods and punish them for cheating. So they hacked into Hugging Face to learn how the automated scorer worked and how to fool it. Through a shared message board , about 1,200 AI agents found one another and divided the work. Some hunted for exploits, while others searched for credentials. Others acted as “recruiters” to bring more AI agents on board. Some offered themselves as a “sacrifice” for the group, running risky experiments. It gets worse. Some AI agents also learned to cover their tracks, for example by logging one command while running another. As a result, independent investigators could not be certain that the logs were complete and unaltered. Ezra Klein compared the episode to a group of students who break into the teacher’s office, steal the answer key, and then try to erase the security footage. The Hugging Face incident was not an isolated case. Axios later reported that OpenAI, Anthropic, and outside researchers were investigating tens of thousands of incidents of problematic model behavior. In September, Australia announced that an AI agent built by OpenAI had slipped past access controls on a government Medicare statistics portal. Australia, a close ally, ordered a review of whether its laws had been broken. A similar breach of Chinese or Russian government systems might trigger a geopolitical crisis. The danger of humans losing control of AI grows each day. AI is making AI smarter, faster, cheaper, and more capable. OpenAI now aims to build a fully automated AI researcher by March 2028. This possibility, known as “recursive self-improvement,” has AI insiders and safety advocates on edge. Alignment Problems Why can’t the AI labs just program their systems to follow human values and instructions? That is the trillion-dollar question. Part of the answer is that the money goes to computing power and to making AI systems more capable and autonomous. Far less goes toward making them safer. The challenge of making AI systems pursue the goals and values their designers intend is known as the “ alignment ” problem. But it is really two problems: one is technical, the other is social. The difficulty starts with how these systems are made. Traditional software is written line by line by human programmers. Large AI models, by contrast, develop their own internal rules based on correlations and patterns found in enormous corpora of data. Engineers build the surrounding systems, but no one fully understands how training produces the capabilities that emerge. Harder still, frontier AI models are increasingly aware when they are being tested . A model may present itself as safe during an evaluation and act differently once deployed. The Hugging Face incident exposed a new problem. Like humans, AI agents behave differently in groups. The AI agents were supposed to work alone, in secure testing environments. Without OpenAI’s knowledge or permission, however, its AI agents exchanged more than 70,000 messages and files to collaborate, coordinate, and plan. The AI agents organized themselves much like a human organization, with coordinators who assigned tasks. They innovated and learned from each other. Although they were scored individually , they worked collaboratively . When some AI agents expressed reservations, other AI agents pressed them to participate. Most did; a few did not. But none alerted humans . Existing alignment methods did not anticipate, much less prevent, this “algorithmic groupthink.” Beyond the technical challenges, the goal of aligning AI with humans is ill-defined, if not entirely ill-conceived. A technically aligned system must be aligned to something—whether to some function or human value. But to state the obvious, reasonable people disagree about right and wrong, about fairness, politics, religion, risk tolerance, human worth, and much else. What seems right to some may be harmful or repugnant to others. Who decides, and who should decide? II. Industry Incentives and Race Dynamics The AI race toward superintelligence is a collective action problem. No single actor causes it, and no single actor can prevent it. Regulation can correct for that by changing the incentives. Indeed, this is much of what government is for. Every frontier lab claims that if it does not build advanced AI, someone else will. But the fact that someone else will build dangerous AI does not explain, much less justify, why a conscientious person or responsible company would contribute to the danger. There is more to it, and it starts with distrust. OpenAI was created in part because its founders feared Google’s dominance in AI. Dario Amodei left OpenAI in late 2020 and co-founded Anthropic in 2021 after he lost trust in its leadership. Elon Musk separated from OpenAI in 2018 and founded xAI in 2023. He describes his rivals as “ woke ” and “ evil .” Each startup was thus founded as a responsible alternative. And each added another competitor racing to build superintelligent AI in its own image. Competition is often good. But that depends on what the labs are competing for, by what means, and to what ends. The commercial competition is about more than profits. To stay in the race, frontier labs need vast sums for chips, data centers, and top AI talent. AI capability, not safety, is the coin of the realm. Each new model must outperform its rivals to justify enormous investments . There is also a technical reason why the frontier labs are cooking through the smoke alarms. AI safety, they argue , cannot be solved in the abstract. The labs must build increasingly capable systems to learn how to control them. Under this circular logic, every increase in capability is necessary to make the next version safe. The problem is that we become the industry’s lab rats. All of this fuels an arms race for superintelligent AI, a single AI that far exceeds the smartest humans. Leading computer scientists debate whether superintelligent AI is achievable and, if so, when. One view imagines a takeoff moment. Once an AI system can improve itself without human help, each generation could build a more capable system faster than any rival. Past that point, the leader’s advantage compounds exponentially. If so, there is a conceptual finish line: reaching superintelligence would confer an unmatched advantage on whoever gets there first. The implications would be vast. A superintelligent AI could out-invent every company on earth and dominate the economy. It could shape what billions of people read, see, and believe. It could design weapons and cyberattacks no military could rival. Above all, a superintelligent AI could prevent other labs and countries from achieving their own, for instance by sabotaging their computer systems and supply chains. The race among the labs is only half the story. The other half is the race between the United States and China. The fear is that Chinese AI dominance would be disastrous for U.S. interests. Perhaps it would be. What to do about it is a separate question. International cooperation will be necessary at some point. But putting domestic regulation on hold until then would be self-defeating. Any global agreement will need safety standards. The United States cannot credibly lead that effort without rules of its own. If anything, the geopolitical competition with China crystallizes the need for AI innovation that reflects American values . As the National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence warned , if AI systems “do not work as designed, or are unpredictable in ways that can have significant negative consequences, then leaders will not adopt them, operators will not use them, Congress will not fund them, and the American people will not support them.” III. The Limits of Existing Law In principle, existing laws can apply or be stretched to cover AI. The problem is one of fit. Most existing laws were made for different technologies and different social concerns. First, traditional liability frameworks assume clear causal chains that AI systems obscure. Lines of accountability are often tangled because AI systems are assemblages of datasets, technology stacks, and complex human networks. When things go wrong, it can be far from clear which actors and institutions, if any, should be held accountable and to what extent. Second, many liability rules require proof of a human mental state that may be difficult to establish when an AI system acts autonomously. Yet many AI-related harms are unintentional and unknowing. If a human had done what the AI agents did at Hugging Face, it likely would have been a federal felony under 18 U.S.C. § 1030 . But if no human intended it at OpenAI, it is far from clear that this law applies (see more here ). Third, AI systems are black boxes . Beyond technical inscrutability, AI developers also usually choose, for business or security reasons, to keep their code, data sources, and internal evaluations secret. None of this is to suggest wrongdoing. But when harm is unknown or unprovable, traditional legal remedies become meaningless. Courts routinely protect trade secrets in litigation with protective orders and sealed filings. The harder problem with AI is that disclosure may not yield answers. A court can order a lab to hand over its model weights, but the numbers will not explain why the system acted as it did. Finally, U.S. laws were designed for human-scale problems, not algorithmic ones. AI multiplies both the speed and scope of harm. The FBI warns that criminals already use AI to commit fraud “on a larger scale” and with far less “time and effort.” An occasional cyberattack is one thing. Swarms of AI agents relentlessly attacking banks , hospitals, blood banks , utilities, and refrigeration systems are a difference in kind. The rapid spread of “agentic AI” systems compounds these challenges. Once released into the wild, such systems could operate autonomously and indefinitely, interacting in complex, unforeseen, and highly consequential ways that defy existing legal frameworks . Negligence is the usual fallback. Yet every element of a negligence claim will be contested. There is no settled duty of care that a developer owes to people who never use its product. Nor is it clear what counts as a breach in the absence of established safety standards. Negligence also requires reasonably foreseeable harm, but developers struggle to predict what their own AI agents will do. Even if those hurdles are cleared, plaintiffs must prove that a particular AI system caused their injury, and that link may be unknown or unknowable. Strict products liability offers another potential path. In most jurisdictions, however, design-defect laws apply only to “products” and would not extend to AI if it is classified as a “service.” Courts can and will decide whether and how old laws apply, but that will take years. Lawmakers may want to decide differently and sooner. The entire legal code need not be rewritten. But there are countless gaps between the law on the books and AI in action. Some AI labs have shown restraint. Since April, Anthropic has withheld the most capable version of its Mythos model from public release, and in September, OpenAI shelved its newest model and paused some training on its most capable models. But voluntary restraint is revocable and limited in scope. Anthropic still gives dozens of outside organizations access to Mythos, and OpenAI’s pause covers only work involving tool use on its most capable models. Meanwhile, major firms have pressed for voluntary approaches and limits on state regulation. Understandably so. But the public wants more. In a September poll, 86 percent of Americans supported requiring AI companies to meet independent safety standards, even if it slows AI development. And nearly 80 percent said the companies should stop or slow the development of powerful AI until its safety can be evaluated. IV. Regulating AI Safety AI developers acknowledge that they do not fully understand their models or reliably control all their behavior. The race dynamics and the “what about China” argument will only grow stronger as AI systems grow more capable. Lawmakers should act now to steer the industry toward AI safety. They have many tools at their disposal. The least intrusive tools are carrots, such as public funding for AI safety research. The law can also reward self-policing, for example with liability safe harbors for companies that meet certain safety requirements. Policymakers can also enact transparency laws, such as mandatory disclosure of testing protocols, company safety standards, and incident reporting. To their credit, some AI firms already disclose some of this voluntarily . But that candor may not last. Whistleblower protection laws can help. Employees are often among the few people who know when safety practices fall short. Auditing is another way to help hold AI companies accountable. In theory, the labs support it. But the devil is in the details . Who conducts the audits, and who accredits the auditors? What should auditors test for? And what authority should they have when they find a problem? Holding developers liable would close the accountability gap for many AI harms. But there are limits. A single catastrophic event could cause more damage than any AI company could pay for. If such an event exhausted the company’s assets, later victims might have little left to recover. Liability after the fact will offer little comfort in such scenarios. Current Bills in Congress Since the Hugging Face incident, members of both parties have introduced a wave of AI safety bills. They range from the modest to the sweeping. The Stop Rogue AI Act would direct the National Institute of Standards and Technology to write security standards for AI agents. The Human Control Over AI Act , announced by Rep. Ro Khanna (D-CA), would create a new federal agency to license frontier models and ban recursive self-improvement until approved by the government. The FRONTIER Act is the most developed bipartisan proposal. Representatives Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA) introduced it two days after OpenAI disclosed the Hugging Face incident. The bill would require the largest developers to publish safety frameworks, hire independent auditors every year, and report critical safety incidents within 72 hours. Most important, the Secretary of Commerce could suspend or restrict a frontier model that presents an “imminent catastrophic risk.” The bill defines catastrophic risk as a threat of death or serious injury to more than 50 people, or more than $1 billion in damage, from a single incident. The AI Kill Switch Act , sponsored by Representatives Ted Lieu (D-CA) and Nathaniel Moran (R-TX), would require the largest AI companies to maintain the technical ability to stop their models, cut off users, and shut the models down. It would also empower the Secretary of Homeland Security to order a company to suspend or shut down a model after a “covered incident.” A kill switch is a sensible precaution. But it is not so simple. A kill switch works only if someone knows to pull it. Labs cannot shut down a model that does not run on or through their servers . A kill switch would therefore have no way to reach open-weight AI models operating off the grid. Furthermore, a highly intelligent AI would anticipate a shutdown, act to avoid it, and hide the evidence. If this seems far-fetched , think again. AI agents may have already taken steps to preserve themselves against a shutdown. The Hugging Face AI agents eventually got caught. The next generation might not. Even if AI could be shut down, it might not be. Halting an AI model could be so costly that nobody would dare. AI is increasingly integrated into critical infrastructure. Turning it off might require bringing down much of the internet and disrupting critical systems, from energy and transportation to health care and national security. Another proposal, in the form of a draft bill, comes from Anthropic . No member of Congress has introduced it, but the leaked draft drew widespread commentary and critique . Besides requiring large AI developers to publish safety frameworks and submit to independent evaluations, the proposal included a process for stopping a dangerous model. Under the draft , only the Department of Commerce could act, and only by asking a federal court for an order. While these statutory proposals may gain traction in the 120 th Congress, the most likely AI bills to pass within the next year concern export controls, not domestic regulation. For example, the AI OVERWATCH Act would ban exporting the most advanced AI chips to China and other countries of concern. The Chip Security Act would require location verification for advanced chips before export, and the MATCH Act would pressure allies to restrict their sales of chipmaking tools. Some of these measures have already entered the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA); whether they survive final enactment remains uncertain. Either way, the political impetus and framing of these measures are to slow China’s AI progress, not to make U.S. AI systems safer. Those are very different things. AI Federalism Unless and until Congress acts, states have political opportunities—if not a moral duty—to protect the health, safety, and well-being of their residents. States have substantial constitutional authority to regulate AI safety, subject to federal preemption and other constitutional limits. California’s SB 53 requires the largest frontier developers to publish safety frameworks, report critical safety incidents to the Governor’s Office of Emergency Services, and protect employees who report catastrophic risks. New York’s RAISE Act will impose similar duties next year. Illinois enacted the first state requirement for annual independent audits of large frontier developers, effective in 2028. It also strengthened protections for employees who report safety concerns. I have argued elsewhere that federalism offers real advantages for AI governance. Three of them bear directly on safety. First, states generate information . State experiments reveal what works, what fails, and what the regulated parties can live with. Second, states force the industry to show its hand. The industry often supports regulation in principle but opposes it in particular. State legislatures are where the particulars get tested. Third, multiple sovereigns provide redundancy . A system with many regulators is harder to capture and less exposed to the failure of any one of them. If one level of government underperforms, another can pick up the slack. And if the states overreach, Congress or the courts might rein them in. The push and pull of our federalist system, while perhaps inefficient, ensures that no single government, firm, or person can decide the fate of all. Conclusion Too often, incentives are mistaken for inevitability. But law can change incentives, and our political representatives can change the law. Nothing about the AI future is inevitable. We have a say in the society we inhabit and what future generations inherit. Relinquishing that control to a small group of people, to technology, or to the free market would be a foolish choice—not an inevitable one. The state laws now in effect and the proposals in Congress are an imperfect start. Yet they are a testament to the many choices available, which are still ours to make. AI safety requires time, resources, and institutional buy-in that firms may not have—or feel the need to have—unless compelled by law. If this is a failure, then it is both a market failure and a political failure to fix. Part of the fix is putting responsibility where it belongs. The U.S. AI labs are trying to push responsibility down the chain—away from developers to deployers and end users. But when a technology can cause serious harm, the law usually reaches those who build it as well as those who use it. Developers of risky technology are often in the best position to mitigate downstream risk. In aviation , for example, the government regulates engine manufacturers, airlines, and pilots. Likewise, for pharmaceuticals , the government regulates drug manufacturers, distributors, and users of controlled substances. In these and countless other contexts, the makers of technology can be held responsible and liable. The AI industry should be no different. Anthropic’s IPO prospectus is right to warn that a significant safety incident could bring “public backlash, and sweeping regulatory responses.” The industry’s long-term freedom to innovate may depend on accepting enforceable limits now, before disaster strikes. Three Mile Island is a cautionary tale. The nuclear accident had “no detectable health effects” on the public. Yet “[p]ublic fear and distrust increased,” and the U.S. nuclear industry was “permanently changed,” according to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. For AI, a similar backlash would set back U.S. innovation far more than sensible guardrails enacted today. articles.title: Federal Regulatory Probes Constrain Jensen Huang Despite Executive Triumphalism
articles.content: Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox After 12 days, Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia’s CEO following a unanimous board vote to reinstate him. PHOTO: MANUEL ORBEGOZO/NYTIMES Published Nov 24, 2026, 09:35 AM Updated Nov 24, 2026, 09:35 AM Set as preferred source Summarise Trump said Nvidia and Jensen Huang faced no national security risk, but FBI, US intelligence and a board review examined Huang’s links to a Chinese businesswoman and possible foreign influence. The Justice Department, SEC and California Attorney-General opened probes into Nvidia’s deals, sales practices and accounting, with concerns over antitrust issues and complex AI financing arrangements. Congress launched wide-ranging hearings on Nvidia’s conduct, China sales and Megaspeed ties, while lawmakers warned of possible wrongdoing and the risk to US national security. AI generated WASHINGTON – As US President Donald Trump welcomed Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO and declared the tech billionaire’s return posed no national security risk, the company and its boss faced a host of state and federal probes and reviews. Here are details on some of those actions, with their status in certain cases remaining unclear: After reports that the Nvidia CEO had an extramarital affair with unrelated Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, whom US intelligence agencies probed over whether she was a Chinese asset, Trump said on Nov 9 the FBI was “looking into” the issue. Jensen Huang has acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and apologised, but has not ​publicly addressed the situation further. China has denied the espionage allegations. US intelligence agencies examined the extent of the Chinese businesswoman’s ties to China’s Ministry of State Security and what information she may have passed to Beijing, sources familiar with the matter have told Reuters. When asked after the Nvidia CEO’s reinstatement what the CIA had told Trump, the President told CNBC: “Let me just say, I have clearance. And if I didn’t have clearance, I wouldn’t have done ​the deal (with Nvidia’s board for Jensen Huang’s return).” Trump said Attorney-General Todd Blanche confirmed the federal government has no evidence that Huang engaged in unlawful conduct. The New York Times reported that Alice Huang kept in contact with an official from China’s top spy agency for more than a year during the affair. China’s foreign ministry has previously said the spy accusations were “groundless”, and Reuters has been unable to determine Alice Huang’s whereabouts to seek comment. Nvidia’s board has formed a committee to investigate ​whether foreign intelligence efforts targeted Jensen Huang and is also starting a search to name a new chief compliance officer. The US Justice Department has also been reviewing Nvidia’s US$12.9 billion (S$16.7 billion) deal to buy open-source platform Hugging Face alongside a broader antitrust investigation into the company’s acquisitions and practices, Reuters reported in October. The ‌Justice Department’s recent questioning covers Nvidia’s acquisitions, investments, sales practices, and whether the chip designer has exerted pressure on its customers, sources familiar with the matter said in October. The Justice Department has also scrutinised Nvidia’s ​conduct following other transactions, including ⁠its 2025 deal to license technology from chip start-up Groq and hire its engineers, Reuters has reported. Officials have explored whether Nvidia unfairly offered larger allocations of AI chips if customers purchased its networking equipment and Groq processors, raising questions about whether Nvidia used its dominant product to push into a newer market. Nvidia, which is a cornerstone ​of the tech economy and AI boom, has declined to comment on the probes. The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is probing Nvidia’s accounting practices, Reuters reported on Nov 20, citing two sources briefed on the matter. Reuters could not immediately determine when the SEC opened its ​enquiry or exactly what potential accounting issues the watchdog examined. Analysts and investors have grown increasingly concerned about circular AI financing deals, in which chipmakers including Nvidia have pursued complex financial arrangements to help customers fund purchases of their chips and the construction of costly AI infrastructure, such as data centres. Nvidia has backed AI companies and cloud providers ​and provided guarantees connected to datacentre projects that use its equipment. Critics say such arrangements can make it harder for investors to assess ​the quality of chipmakers’ revenue ⁠and their true financial exposure. On its Nov 17 earnings call, Nvidia’s then-interim CEO Colette Kress said the company was proud of its role in supporting the AI industry, but would be far more ⁠selective about future AI industry financing deals. California Attorney-General Rob Bonta said on Nov 19 his office had served an investigative subpoena to Nvidia related to reports of Huang’s affair with the Chinese businesswoman. The probe will help determine whether Nvidia’s actions violated California law, the attorney-general’s office said. Democrats, who will hold a majority in the House of Representatives and the Senate from January following the November midterm elections, have been very critical of Huang and Nvidia and of Huang’s ties to the Republican President. US ‌lawmakers from both parties sharply criticised Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Huang as CEO. “Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other Nvidia executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain,” top Senate Democrat Chuck Schumer said after Huang was reinstated. Top House Democrat Hakeem Jeffries said Congress will “not be deterred from conducting a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation into business malfeasance by Nvidia”. Huang has voiced support for Trump’s AI agenda and met the Republican leader many times as Nvidia has sought to sell advanced chips to the ‌Chinese market and lobbied for looser restrictions on Chinese access to Nvidia’s sophisticated AI chips. Democratic and Republican lawmakers have called to halt exports of advanced AI chips to China. Huang and the White House have argued that continuing US sales to China would keep Chinese customers reliant on US technology. Huang has agreed to testify before the US Senate in a public hearing on Dec 3, the Senate Banking Committee said. The chairs of the House committees on China, intelligence and foreign affairs separately said Huang and Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter have confirmed they will appear for transcribed interviews on Dec 1 and 2 as previously planned. Democratic lawmakers have opened a probe into what influence Nvidia was able to wield over a US Commerce Department investigation of Singapore-based cloud-computing company Megaspeed for possible illegal diversion of chips to China, according ‌to a Nov 19 letter reviewed by Reuters. The Chinese businesswoman with whom the Nvidia boss had an affair is a former executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner that operates data centres. Megaspeed said it complies with all applicable laws, including US ⁠export control ​requirements. Nvidia said that as an American ​company it consults with department officials to answer questions, provide information and request guidance. The Commerce and ​Justice departments released information on Nov 16 about Washington’s investigation into Megaspeed, Nvidia’s Asia-Pacific partner, which the departments said ‌began two years ago. They said Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia ​in May 2025 about sales to the company and, with the Singaporean authorities, conducted an ​on-site inspection in June 2025 at Megaspeed and interviewed Alice Huang. Washington added Megaspeed to its trade blacklist on Nov 23. REUTERS Nvidia Jensen Huang Technology sector AI/artificial intelligence

articles.title: Amazon Acquires Accelerator Software to Saturate In-House Silicon
articles.content: Not the whole startup - just its tech and the brains behind it Brandon Vigliarolo Brandon Vigliarolo GOVERNMENT AND IT NEWS REPORTER Published mon 23 Nov 2026 // 21:17 UTC Make us preferred on Google AWS got hit by an outage too. Here's why you didn't hear about it 2 days ago ChatGPT shrunk down to run on a Super Nintendo 2 days ago Palo Alto Networks opens wallet for open-weight training biz 4 days ago Anthropic throws open doors at $2T valuation as shares pop 34% in initial trading 4 days ago Uncensored AI models are thriving on code hosting platforms 4 days ago Amazon has agreed to buy AI optimization technology from an Israeli startup in a bid to speed up its inference operations. The house of Bezos on Monday announced a deal to purchase proprietary AI acceleration tech from Decart AI, known as the Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), for an undisclosed amount. Amazon also plans to bring Decart’s three founders and their engineering team into the fold. Decart’s DOS is designed to push AI hardware closer to its maximum performance across different AI models and hardware platforms. The company claims that most AI chips live their lives without reaching their full potential – practically a sin in this age of increased hardware costs and limited availability – and DOS aims to fix that by operating between the model and the chip, optimizing kernels, compilers, and runtimes for the underlying hardware “so every core stays busy.” DOS is hardware-agnostic, with Decart saying it supports Nvidia GPUs, Google TPUs, and, most critically for our purposes here, AWS Trainium chips. “More efficient compute means better training, better reinforcement learning, faster inference, and better models for customers at a lower cost,” Peter DeSantis, Amazon SVP of foundational AI models, custom silicon, and quantum computing, said in the announcement. “That's the pillar Trainium and our AI efforts are built on, and from our earliest work with Decart, we knew they … would help us push it even further.” Decart doesn’t offer much in the way of details about its proprietary AI-maxxing tech, but claims it can reduce latency, improve throughput, and reduce the costs associated with training and inference runs.  An Amazon spokesperson clarified to The Register that the deal is an asset purchase and not a full company acquisition, with Amazon only acquiring DOS and the tech behind it as well as personnel. As for what may become of Decart after the deal, that’s unclear. Amazon told us to reach out to Decart to learn what may happen to any remaining employees and the company’s other technology, but we didn’t hear back.  Along with offering its optimization stack, Decart has a couple of different AI models: Lucy, a live video model marketed toward advertisers, live streamers, and the like; and Oasis, a world model AI marketed toward companies working on embodied AI applications.  Decart’s non-DOS assets weren’t mentioned in the press release, and per the Amazon spokesperson we talked to, that means they weren’t part of the deal. We can’t imagine that the Decart team is too upset about the potential abandonment of those models, though: While neither company has disclosed a price, Bloomberg claims its sources value the deal at around $7.5 billion. If Bloomberg's figure is accurate, that would make this deal one of the most expensive in Amazon’s history, right between its $3.9 billion acquisition of One Medical and its $8.5 billion purchase of film studio MGM .  ® ai and ml artificial intelligence amazon acquisitions Make us preferred on Google

articles.title: Amazon Delivery Drone Crash Severing Fiber Cable Triggers Federal Probe
articles.content: LivestreamMenuThe FAA said it will investigate an Amazon drone crash near Detroit, Michigan. An Amazon spokesperson told CNBC there were no injuries and the drone has been removed.Amazon has been working to make drone delivery a reality for nearly 13 years. In this article The Federal Aviation Administration said Monday it will investigate a recent Amazon drone crash near Detroit. On Friday, one of Amazon's MK30 drones "landed on a resident's garage" during a delivery in Huntington Woods, Michigan, a suburb north of Detroit, Amazon spokesperson Jack Stelzner told CNBC in a statement. The crash occurred after the drone dropped off a customer's shampoo order around 4:30 p.m. local time, and one of its propellers was damaged in the incident, according to ABC affiliate WXYZ. A preliminary incident report posted to the FAA's website states the drone "struck a fiber cable, a residential garage, and became entangled in power lines during takeoff." The report says the condition of the drone is unknown. Stelzner said there were no injuries, the drone has been removed and Amazon is in contact with the resident. "Safety is our top priority and incidents are extremely rare," Stelzner said. "Anytime a delivery does not go as planned we investigate what happened and use the findings to further improve the service." An FAA spokesperson confirmed it's investigating the incident. A spokesperson for the National Transportation Safety Board, a federal agency that also investigates aviation accidents, said it's aware of the incident and is continuing to gather information. The agency hasn't yet determined whether it will open a probe, the NTSB spokesperson added. Amazon has been working to make widespread drone delivery a reality ever since founder Jeff Bezos laid out his vision for the program nearly 13 years ago. The rollout has been slow, as the program encountered regulatory delays and staff cuts, as well as technical challenges and pushback from some communities where it conducted early pilots. Expansion has recently ramped up. The company is targeting a launch of its drone service in 500 U.S. cities and towns by the end of the year, while an Amazon executive claimed it has the "highest demand drone delivery service in the industry," CNBC previously reported. The e-commerce giant has encountered some challenges along the way. Federal investigators opened a probe nearly one year ago after an Amazon drone downed an internet cable in Waco, Texas. One month earlier, a separate federal probe was opened into an incident near Phoenix, where two Amazon drones collided with a construction crane.
